pattern: (remaining connection slots|too many connections|connection pool.*(exhaust|full|timeout)|connection is not available|unable to acquire.*connection|pool.*timed out|max_connections)
cause: The database connection pool is exhausted: requests are queueing for a connection faster than connections are released.
fix: Look for connection leaks or long-held transactions in the code that changed just before onset; roll it back if a deploy lines up.
Check live usage: SELECT count(*), state FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY state; (or SHOW PROCESSLIST on MySQL).
Short term, raise the pool size / max_connections within what the database can serve, or put a pooler such as PgBouncer in front.
Add a connection acquisition timeout and a pool-saturation alert so the next one is caught early.

pattern: (slow query|statement timeout|lock wait timeout|deadlock detected|canceling statement|long[- ]running (query|transaction))
cause: Database queries are slow or blocked on locks, holding connections and backing work up behind them.
fix: Find the offending statements with the slow query log or pg_stat_statements and EXPLAIN them.
Look for a missing index, a lock held by a long transaction, or a migration running on a hot table.
Set statement and lock timeouts so one bad query can't stall the pool.

pattern: (out of memory|oom-kill|oom_reaper|killed process|cannot allocate memory|java\.lang\.outofmemoryerror|memoryerror|memory cgroup out of memory)
cause: A process ran out of memory and was killed (or failed to allocate), which restarts or drops whatever it was serving.
fix: Identify the victim and its peak RSS in the kernel log (dmesg | grep -i 'killed process').
Check for a leak or an unbounded cache/queue introduced recently; compare memory graphs against the last deploy.
Right-size the memory limit, add swap or headroom as a stopgap, and alert on memory pressure before the OOM killer acts.

pattern: (no space left on device|disk quota exceeded|filesystem.*full|write failed.*disk|errno 28)
cause: A filesystem is full, so writes (logs, temp files, database data) are failing.
fix: Find the full mount (df -h) and the biggest consumers (du -xh --max-depth=2 /var | sort -h | tail).
Free space safely: rotate or compress logs, clear package and temp caches, remove stale core dumps.
Fix log rotation or retention so it doesn't refill, and alert at 80% usage.

pattern: (too many open files|emfile|file table overflow|socket: too many)
cause: The process hit its open file descriptor limit, so new sockets and files can't be opened.
fix: Check the current usage (ls /proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l) against the limit (ulimit -n, LimitNOFILE in the unit file).
Look for a descriptor leak: unclosed sockets, files, or connections pooled without a cap.
Raise LimitNOFILE as a stopgap once you know the leak is not the cause.

pattern: (i/o error|blk_update_request|read-only file system|remounting filesystem read-only|ext4-fs error|xfs.*(corruption|metadata))
cause: The storage layer is reporting I/O errors or has remounted read-only, which usually means a failing disk, volume, or controller.
fix: Check SMART / cloud volume health and the kernel log for the device named in the errors.
Move the workload off the affected volume, then run fsck once it is unmounted.
Restore from backup if data was lost; replace the device.

pattern: (temporary failure in name resolution|could not resolve|name or service not known|nxdomain|servfail|unknown host|getaddrinfo.*(failed|enotfound))
cause: Name resolution is failing, so services can't find their dependencies.
fix: Test from the affected host: dig <name> and check /etc/resolv.conf and the resolver's own logs.
Look for a resolver outage, a changed record, or a rate-limited upstream DNS server.
Add a local caching resolver and retry with backoff so a blip doesn't cascade.

pattern: (connection refused|econnrefused|no route to host|network is unreachable|connection reset by peer)
cause: A dependency is refusing or dropping connections: it is down, not yet listening, or blocked by a firewall.
fix: Check that the target service is running and listening (systemctl status, ss -ltnp).
Review firewall / security group changes and recent restarts of the dependency.
Add health checks and retry with backoff so dependents wait out restarts.

cause: A TLS certificate is expired, invalid, or untrusted, so secure connections are being rejected.
fix: Inspect the certificate: openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host | openssl x509 -noout -dates.
Renew or redeploy the certificate and restart whatever caches it.
Automate renewal and alert at 21 days before expiry.

pattern: (segfault|core dumped|signal 11|main process exited|failed with result|start request repeated too quickly|crashed|panic:)
cause: A process is crashing and being restarted, interrupting work in flight.
fix: Pull the crash details: journalctl -u <unit> -b, coredumpctl info.
Correlate the first crash with a deploy or config change and roll it back if they match.
Capture a core dump or stack trace and fix the crash; add a restart back-off so a crash loop can't hammer dependencies.

cause: Requests are being rate limited, either by this service protecting itself or by an upstream provider.
fix: Identify who is being limited and whether traffic grew or a client started retrying aggressively.
Add client-side backoff with jitter and request quotas; raise limits only if the load is legitimate.

pattern: (failed password|authentication failure|invalid user|too many authentication failures)
cause: A burst of failed logins, consistent with credential guessing against the host.
fix: Check the source addresses (they are collapsed in the signature; grep the raw log) and block abusers with fail2ban or firewall rules.
Disable password logins in favour of keys and restrict SSH to known networks.

cause: Operations are failing on permissions, typically after a deploy, ownership change, or policy update.
fix: Check ownership and modes on the path or resource named in the error, and any SELinux/AppArmor denials (ausearch -m avc).
Compare with the last known-good configuration and restore the permissions.

pattern: (upstream timed out|gateway time-?out|upstream prematurely closed|upstream.*(failed|unavailable)|bad gateway|service unavailable| 50[234] )
cause: The front end is timing out talking to an upstream service. This is a symptom; the cause is whatever is making the upstream slow or unavailable.
fix: Look at the other signatures that began just before these errors: the upstream's own errors usually name the cause.

pattern: (request (timed out|timeout)|timed out after|read timed out|deadline exceeded|timeout waiting)
cause: Calls are timing out. This is a symptom of a slow or unreachable dependency.
fix: Find the dependency being called and check its health and saturation.
